Data Visualization with ggplot2

This lab focuses on data visualization and how to create high quality graphics using the ggplot2 package. In this lab we will use cleaned data, with subsequent labs covering how to manipulate data prior to graphing. Much of this will be extremely familiar from your STA209 class, but we will get into more fine control and the nuts-and-bolts of how ggplot2 is actually working.

NOTE: More material will be added to this lab on Wednesday.

\(~\)

Preamble

Packages and Datasets

This lab will use the ggplot2 package:

# install.packages("ggplot2")
library(ggplot2)

It will also use data from The College Scorecard:

colleges <- read.csv("https://nfriedrichsen.github.io/data/Colleges2019.csv")
  • Description: The colleges data set contains attributes and outcomes for all primarily undergraduate institutions in the United States with at least 400 full-time students for the year 2019.

\(~\)

How ggplot2 creates graphics

The ggplot2 package builds graphics in a structured manner using layers. Layers are sequentially added to a graph, with each serving a particular purpose, such as:

  1. Displaying raw data
  2. Displaying a statistical summary
  3. Adding metadata (ie: annotations, context, references, etc.)

Consider the following examples:

## Example #1.1 - nothing (just a base layer)
ggplot(data = colleges, mapping = aes(x = Cost, y = Net_Tuition))

## Example #1.2 - add a layer displaying raw data
ggplot(data = colleges, mapping = aes(x = Cost, y = Net_Tuition)) +
  geom_point()

## Example #1.3 - add another layer (smoother)
ggplot(data = colleges, mapping = aes(x = Cost, y = Net_Tuition)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_smooth()

## Example #1.4 - add another layer (reference text)
ggplot(data = colleges, mapping = aes(x = Cost, y = Net_Tuition)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_smooth() + 
  annotate("text", x = 20000, y = 40000, label = "Data from 2019")

Note: A high-quality graphic doesn’t require any particular number of layers. In fact, more layers can sometimes detract from the clarity of a data visualization.

\(~\)

More on the base layer

The mapping and data arguments provided in the base layer are carried forward to all subsequent layers. This is often desirable, but we can also specify or change aesthetics within an individual layer.

Consider the difference between the following two graphs:

## Color is mapped to Region
ggplot(data = colleges, mapping = aes(x = Cost, y = Net_Tuition, color = Region)) +
  geom_point()

## Every point is set to red
ggplot(data = colleges, mapping = aes(x = Cost, y = Net_Tuition, color = Region)) +
  geom_point(color = "red")

In the first graph, color = Region appears inside aes(). This tells ggplot2 that color should represent information contained in the variable Region.

In the second graph, color = "red" appears outside aes(). This does not represent another variable. Instead, it simply instructs ggplot2 to draw every point in red.

Aesthetics can also be specified locally within individual layers:

## Example #2.1
ggplot(data = colleges) +
  geom_point(mapping = aes(x = Cost, y = Net_Tuition)) 

## Example #2.2
ggplot(data = colleges) +
  geom_point(mapping = aes(x = Cost, y = Net_Tuition)) +
  geom_point(mapping = aes(x = Cost, y = Enrollment), color = "red")

Local specification is useful when different layers of a graph need to display different variables or use different aesthetics.

\(~\)

Creating Effective Visualizations

The fundamental principles of creating effective data visualizations are quite simple. In short, an effective visualization should:

  1. Clearly convey a particular message
  2. Let the data speak for itself with minimal distortion
  3. Avoid “sales tactics” and unnecessary frills

It’s helpful to understand these principles with a few examples of effective and ineffective visuals.

The Grammar of ggplot2

The ggplot framework is unique because graphics are grammatically defined. Two of the most important pieces are:

  • Aesthetics (or “aes”) - mappings of variables to visual properties such as position, color, or size.
  • Geometric elements (or “geoms”) - what you actually see in the plot, such as points, lines, bars, or curves.

For example:

ggplot(data = colleges, mapping = aes(x = Cost, y = Net_Tuition, color = Region)) +
  geom_point()

Here, Cost, Net_Tuition, and Region are mapped to the aesthetics x, y, and color. The points themselves are created using geom_point().

Different geoms can display the same variables in different ways, and different types of variables naturally lend themselves to different geoms.

Question #1

Consider the graph below:

ggplot(data = colleges,
       mapping = aes(x = Cost, y = Net_Tuition, color = Type)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_smooth()

A. Which variables are mapped to the x, y, and color aesthetics?

B. What geometric elements are being displayed?

C. What happens if you move color = Type from the ggplot() function into geom_point()? Run the modified code and briefly describe the difference.

\(~\)

Mapping versus Setting Aesthetics

Remember that placing an aesthetic inside aes() maps a variable to that aesthetic:

ggplot(colleges, aes(x = Cost, y = Net_Tuition, color = Region)) +
  geom_point()

In contrast, specifying something like color = "red" outside aes() simply changes the appearance of the geom:

ggplot(colleges, aes(x = Cost, y = Net_Tuition)) +
  geom_point(color = "red")

This distinction applies to other visual properties as well.

Facets

Adding more aesthetics is one way to display additional variables, but graphs can quickly become difficult to interpret when too many things are displayed at once.

Facets allow us to break the data into separate plots according to one or more categorical variables.

  • facet_wrap() displays separate panels according to one categorical variable.
  • facet_grid() displays panels corresponding to combinations of two categorical variables.

Consider the following examples:

reduced_colleges = subset(
  colleges,
  Region %in% c("Great Lakes", "Far West", "Plains")
)

## facet_wrap
ggplot(data = reduced_colleges, aes(x = Cost)) +
  geom_density() +
  facet_wrap(~Region, nrow = 1)

## facet_grid
ggplot(data = reduced_colleges, aes(x = Cost)) +
  geom_density() +
  facet_grid(Type ~ Region)

The facet_wrap() function wraps a series of plots according to a fixed number of rows or columns, while facet_grid() constructs a grid based upon combinations of the variables supplied to it.

Question #4

Create a histogram of Enrollment and facet the graph according to the variable Type.

Then modify your graph so that the histograms are also colored according to Type.

Briefly compare what the color aesthetic and faceting are doing. What information is being represented redundantly?

Compare the distributions of enrollment for the different types of colleges.

\(~\)

Question #5

Create a scatterplot showing the relationship between Cost and Net_Tuition.

  • Map Region to the color aesthetic.
  • Display only colleges from the "Great Lakes", "Far West", and "Plains" regions.
  • Use facets to display the three regions in separate panels.
  • Add a smoother to each panel.

Describe the relationship between Cost and Net_Tuition. Does the relationship appear similar across the three regions, or are there differences worth noting?

You may use subset() to restrict the data before constructing your graph.
